notes.meaning: Spring was the normal season when the weather cleared and kings marched out to battle. David sent Joab and the Israelite army to fight the Ammonites, but David stayed behind in Jerusalem. By resting at home instead of leading his men, David placed himself in the path of temptation. Neglecting our duties leaves our hearts unprotected against evil desires.

David got up from his afternoon rest and strolled along the flat roof of his palace in the cool evening. From there, he looked down and saw a very beautiful woman taking a bath in a courtyard. The sight itself was not yet the sin, but David lingered and fed his lust instead of turning his eyes away.

David sent a messenger to find out who the woman was. He was told she was Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite. Her father and her husband were both faithful soldiers in David's elite forces. That knowledge should have stopped David immediately, but his unchecked lust pushed him forward.

David sent messengers to bring Bathsheba to the palace, and he slept with her. The text notes that she had just finished her monthly cleansing ritual, showing that she was not pregnant before this encounter. David abused his royal power to commit adultery, and sin quickly gathered speed.

Bathsheba found out she was pregnant and sent a short message to David to tell him. Under God's law, adultery was a crime punishable by death for both the man and the woman. Her message was an urgent plea for the king to do something before the secret was discovered.

Instead of confessing his wickedness, David immediately tried to cover it up. He ordered Joab to send Uriah back to Jerusalem, and Joab obeyed. David hoped to make it look like Uriah was the father of the unborn child.

When Uriah arrived, David asked him friendly questions about how Joab, the troops, and the war were doing. David pretended to care about the military news, but it was only an excuse to hide his true intentions. Sin often leads people to hide behind false smiles and shallow words.

David told Uriah to go home to his house, rest, and wash his feet after his long trip. The king even sent a royal gift of food after him as a special honor. David wanted Uriah to enjoy an evening with his wife so that the pregnancy would appear normal.

Uriah did not go down to his house, but slept at the palace entrance with the king's guards. God in His providence guided Uriah's actions so that David's hidden crime would not remain buried. Even the most clever schemes of sinners cannot outsmart God's purpose.

The next morning, servants told David that Uriah had not gone home. David asked Uriah why he refused to go to his own house after enduring such a long journey. David's pretend concern was really fear that his cover-up plan was failing.

Uriah told the king that the sacred ark and the armies of Israel were camping out in simple tents in the open field. He swore an oath that he could not enjoy comforts and sleep with his wife while his comrades faced danger and hardship. Uriah's noble devotion and discipline stood in sharp contrast to David's selfish indulgence.

David urged Uriah to stay in the city for one more day, promising to send him back to the army tomorrow. Uriah trusted his king and remained in Jerusalem through that day and the next. David only wanted extra time to invent another way to hide his guilt.

David invited Uriah to eat and drink with him and intentionally got him drunk. David hoped that too much wine would weaken Uriah's resolve and drive him home to his wife. Even while drunk, Uriah maintained his military duty and slept with the guards instead of going home.

The next morning, David wrote a secret letter to Joab and sent it by Uriah's own hand. David relied on Uriah's complete honesty, knowing the loyal soldier would not break the seal to read it. In an act of terrible betrayal, David made an innocent man deliver his own death sentence.

David's letter ordered Joab to place Uriah at the front of the fiercest fighting and then abandon him so he would be killed. Because Uriah refused to compromise his honor, David resolved to take his life. When sin goes unconfessed, it hardens the heart and leads from lust to cold murder.

While laying siege to Rabbah, Joab obeyed David's cruel instructions. He assigned Uriah to lead an assault at the exact spot where he knew the enemy had their strongest fighters. Joab chose to protect his own standing with the king rather than defend an innocent soldier.

The Ammonite defenders charged out of the city and fought Joab's men, killing several Israelite soldiers. Uriah the Hittite died in the battle, exactly as David had planned. David's plot succeeded, but other innocent men died simply to cover up the king's shame.

Joab immediately sent a messenger to Jerusalem to give David a full report of what happened in the battle. He needed to report the military loss and confirm that the king's secret order had been carried out.

Joab gave the messenger careful instructions in case David became angry about the army fighting too close to the city wall. Joab recalled how Prince Abimelech had died long ago when a woman dropped a heavy stone on him from a wall. He told the messenger to calm David's anger by adding that Uriah the Hittite was dead as well. Joab knew that the news of Uriah's death was what the king truly wanted to hear.
The messenger traveled to Jerusalem and delivered the exact report Joab had commanded him to speak. He carried out his duty faithfully without knowing the dark secret behind the king's orders.

The messenger explained that the enemy had charged out into the open field, but the Israelites drove them back to the city gates. Archers on the city walls then shot down on them, killing several royal soldiers along with Uriah the Hittite. Joab's messenger gave David the confirmation he had been waiting to hear.

David sent the messenger back to encourage Joab and told him not to be troubled by the losses. He excused the deaths by claiming that the sword strikes down one person just as easily as another during war. David disguised murder as an ordinary accident of battle, showing how dull his conscience had become.

When Bathsheba learned that her husband was dead, she went through the traditional days of public mourning for him. This mourning period usually lasted for seven days. She completed the expected ritual of sorrow for the faithful man who had been destroyed because of David's sin.

When the days of mourning ended, David brought Bathsheba into his home as his wife, and she gave birth to a son. To the watching world, the king seemed to have managed the crisis and protected his public honor. But the Lord saw every secret deed, and the story closes with the warning that David's actions were thoroughly evil in God's eyes.
